meta.title: Marker-Free Computer-Vision-Driven Autonomous Docking for a Space Interface
meta.authorsHtml: Andoni Benito<sup>∗</sup>, Endika Llano<sup>∗</sup>, Ainhoa Ruiz<sup>∗</sup>, Verónica González

abstract: Automation is becoming indispensable for on-orbit servicing, assembly, and manufacturing, driving the need for standardized robotic interfaces. This work presents a marker-free vision subsystem for the Standard Interface for Robotic Manipulation (SIROM) that provides real-time six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) pose estimation of a passive SIROM relative to its active counterpart. The subsystem relies solely on dual grayscale images from two rigidly mounted cameras and outputs a learned visibility score and the relative pose, represented by Cartesian translation and quaternion orientation. Trained on a 20,000-sample dataset collected with a UR10e manipulator, the model obtains 8.431 mm translational RMSE and 0.0986 rad (5.65◦) C3-symmetry-aware rotational RMSE on the held-out test set; close to the 0.20 m docking decision distance, errors fall to approximately 5 mm and 0.05 rad. Visibility was classified correctly for every test example. At approximately 30 Hz, the system completed autonomous demonstrations under clutter, target motion, and tilted/elevated configurations. These results represent a step toward reliable, marker-independent, vision-only docking for modular space robotics.

blocks.html: The increasing complexity of on-orbit servicing, assembly, and manufacturing demands standardized robotic interfaces that support modular operations. In this context, the Standard Interface for Robotic Manipulation (SIROM) is a standardized interface that provides mechanical, electrical, and data coupling between robotic modules [1]. Several SIROM variants exist (Figure 1); in this work, we focus on the C variant as the target of our docking experiments.

However, fully autonomous docking between the active and passive SIROM units remains challenging. Existing solutions for autonomous docking typically rely on fiducial markers, whose performance degrades under occlusion, suboptimal lighting, or oblique viewing angles [2]. The previous SIROM self-docking system in [2] uses an eye-inhand camera and a dedicated three-marker ArUco board attached to the passive interface; its controller combines position-based visual servoing with an admittance-based force-control phase for final alignment.

We present a marker-free vision subsystem that avoids the need for a dedicated marker board by delivering real-time six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) pose estimation of a passive SIROM relative to its active counterpart. The approach uses synchronized grayscale images from two rigidly mounted cameras to predict a learned visibility score and the relative pose, represented by Cartesian translation and quaternion orientation. Quaternions are adopted for their continuous, singularity-free representation, which avoids discontinuities and is well suited to regression in deep neural networks. The SIROM’s three-fold rotational symmetry is handled explicitly during training and control.

blocks.html: Traditional 6-DoF pose estimation methods are divided into feature-based and template-based approaches. Feature matching can struggle with low texture and occlusion, whereas template methods can be sensitive to viewpoint, illumination, and clutter. Both typically assume known object geometry and need symmetry-aware treatment when several orientations appear identical.

Deep learning has improved RGB-only pose estimation. Direct regression methods such as PoseCNN [3] predict pose from a single image but require object-specific training. Other approaches detect 2D cues and solve PnP, including SSD-6D [4], BB8 [5], Pix2Pose [6], and PVNet [7]; these use explicit geometry and multi-stage pipelines. One-stage models such as EfficientPose [8], depth-based methods such as DenseFusion [9], and foundation models such as FoundationPose [10] offer alternative accuracy–complexity trade-offs.

For autonomous docking, fiducials [11] and geometry-based refinement [12] remain common. The marker-based SIROM demonstrator in [2] is the most relevant system-level reference, but it uses a different camera arrangement, controller, workspace, and validation protocol. Consequently, it is not a numerically matched baseline. Our dualcamera CNN–Transformer instead removes the dedicated fiducial board while applying symmetry-aware learning and temporal smoothing.

The setup employed two monochrome Basler Ace 2 a2A2448-75umBAS cameras equipped with Basler C23- 0824-5M 8 mm lenses. Both cameras were rigidly mounted into the active SIROM, with their fields of view (FOV) overlapping in a way that maximizes the combined FOV, and ensures that the close-up central area is seen by both cameras simultaneously. Automatic gain control and brightness regulation were enabled, allowing consistent exposure and brightness adaptation to varying lighting conditions without manual tuning.

A 20,000-sample dataset was collected using a UR10e manipulator. The passive SIROM was randomly positioned within a bounded workspace, and the robot executed parabolic-helical trajectories to capture diverse viewpoints (Figure 2). Ground-truth relative poses were obtained from robot kinematics and the commanded target placement. Each sample contains a paired grayscale observation and the relative state (x, y, z, qw, qx, qy, qz, v) in the active- SIROM frame, where v ∈{0, 1} is the target-visibility

Table position, in-plane rotation, trajectory origin and height, helix radius and turn count, and sampling density were randomized. The robot executed a broad parabolic– helical sweep followed by a conical close-up trajectory. The fully automated pipeline repositioned the connector, executed motion sequences, and triggered synchronized image capture from both cameras. The data rows were randomly assigned once to 70% training, 20% validation, and 10% test subsets.

Environmental diversity was increased with random objects and printed patterns. Target-absent runs provide the negative class v = 0, while partial obstruction is emulated through training-time augmentation.
Example trajectories and samples are shown in Figure 2, Figure 3, and Figure 4.

blocks.html: Images were resized to a fixed resolution of 512×612 pixels and normalized to balance computational efficiency with sufficient spatial detail for accurate pose estimation. This fixed resolution reduces memory usage, improves throughput, and stabilizes training while preserving the geometric cues required for docking. Single-channel normalization used mean 0.45 and standard deviation 0.27, and images were converted to float tensors. Validation and test images received only this preprocessing.

To enhance robustness, extensive appearance-level data augmentation was applied to training images, including blur effects, synthetic occlusions and dropout, morphological perturbations, and shadowing. Sharpening/compression, illumination and contrast changes, and noise were also applied. These augmentations simulate realistic imaging degradations and partial visibility without altering the underlying scene geometry. Geometric transformations were deliberately avoided to maintain strict consistency between pixel coordinates and ground-truth poses.

The proposed model estimates the spatial state of the passive SIROM—its 3D position, orientation, and visibility— from a pair of synchronized grayscale images. Each image is processed independently by a shared ConvNeXtV2-Atto convolutional backbone, initialized with ImageNet weights and adapted to one input channel, which extracts hierarchical local features such as edges, contours, and structural patterns. The final feature map from each view is flattened into token sequences, linearly projected to 512 dimensions, and augmented with fixed 2D positional encodings and learned camera-segment embeddings.

The combined token sequence is processed by an eight-layer, pre-normalized Transformer encoder with 16 attention heads, 512-dimensional tokens, a 1024-dimensional feed-forward block, and 0.1 dropout. Through selfattention, the Transformer captures long-range spatial dependencies and establishes correspondences both within each view and across views, enabling global reasoning about the connector geometry. A dedicated classification (CLS) token aggregates global scene information into a 512-dimensional embedding that summarizes the spatial configuration of the passive SIROM.

This embedding is passed to three independent multi-layer perceptrons that decode (i) Cartesian translation, (ii) orientation as a unit quaternion, and (iii) a scalar visibility score in the range [0, 1]. Each head has two 1024-unit hidden layers with LeakyReLU activations and layer normalization; the quaternion is normalized to unit length and the visibility head applies a sigmoid. This multi-branch design allows the three tasks to share geometrical understanding capabilities.
The overall network architecture is illustrated in Figure 5, highlighting the dual-image input, feature extraction, Transformer encoding, and separate prediction heads.

Orientation is represented as a unit quaternion to ensure a continuous and numerically stable formulation. Compared to Euler angles and rotation vectors, this representation avoids discontinuities such as gimbal lock and ambiguities arising from multiple equivalent parameterizations. The SIROM’s three-fold rotational symmetry is handled by comparing the prediction with the three orientations separated by 120◦around the connector axis and retaining the smallest geodesic distance.

A multi-component loss jointly optimizes translation, rotation, and visibility. Translation loss is computed as Cartesian MSE. Rotation loss is a squared quaternion geodesic error in rad2, using the nearest equivalent under the SIROM’s three-fold rotational symmetry. Visibility is optimized using binary cross-entropy. Pose losses are computed only when v = 1; target-absent samples train only the visibility head. Loss scales are initialized from trivial predictions and optimized with AdamW and cosine-annealing warm restarts.

blocks.html: After training, the docking pipeline operates in a closed loop, incorporating pose and visibility estimates at each control cycle. To improve robustness, raw poses are not directly averaged over time, as the passive SIROM may have moved and recent samples may correspond to different passive poses. Instead, a motion-aware temporal weighting strategy is applied. The scalar c ∈[0, 1] is a learned visibility-confidence score: its ground truth is v = 1 when the passive SIROM is present in the paired observation and v = 0 for target-absent acquisition samples. At run time, the controller averages the last 20 scores and incorporates low-confidence estimates as higher temporal inconsistency when weighting the pose history.

Pose estimates are expressed in a global reference frame. Consecutive translation and rotation increments— derived from symmetry-consistent quaternion differences— are computed and smoothed over a five-sample window. Smoothing increments rather than absolute poses reduces jitter and suppresses transient outliers while preserving persistent pose changes.

A motion magnitude combining the smoothed translational and rotational increments, modulated by visibility, defines temporal weights that emphasize recent consistent estimates and progressively down-weight older or unreliable samples. When predictions remain stable, their historical influence increases; abrupt deviations automatically reduce the contribution of inconsistent poses.

The final passive pose is obtained via weighted position averaging and weighted quaternion averaging with renormalization and symmetry handling. Using the same weights, the controller computes weighted position/orientation standard deviation and an effective memory length, defined as the number of frames contributing meaningfully to the estimate, over at most 256 recent estimates. These metrics govern transitions between search, approach, align, and dock (Figure 6) through phase-specific thresholds. The search-to-approach transition requires c ≥0.3 and an effective memory of at least 10 frames; approach-to-align requires c ≥0.9 and 35 frames. Before final docking, the controller requires c ≥0.95, at least 40 effective frames, position and orientation standard deviations below 2 mm and 1◦, respectively, and bounded residual hover-pose error. At 30 Hz, the 10-, 35-, and 40frame thresholds correspond to nominal evidence windows of 0.33, 1.17, and 1.33 s, respectively; they are confidenceconvergence gates rather than full manoeuvre times. Low confidence therefore prevents the final docking command and can return the robot to a safer search or approach state. Progress requires sufficiently coherent and well-supported recent estimates, whereas inconsistent predictions reduce memory and may trigger reversion to safer behaviors.

The instantiated network contains 25,119,376 trainable parameters. The model runs at approximately 30 Hz on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090, providing a fresh visual estimate roughly every 33 ms. The model could be quantized for embedded GPUs, although performance on flightrepresentative hardware remains to be validated.

Ten percent of the dataset was reserved for testing. Translation RMSE is the square root of the mean squared 3D Cartesian error and is reported in millimetres, whereas rotational RMSE is the C3-symmetry-aware geodesic error reported in radians. Both pose metrics are calculated only for target-present samples; visibility is evaluated by classification accuracy across all test samples.

The visibility evaluation contains 2,090 paired observations: 1,906 target-present and 184 target-absent pairs. At the c = 0.5 decision threshold, it yields 1,906 true positives and 184 true negatives, with no false positives or false negatives; the corresponding ROC area under the curve is 1.00.

blocks.html: Figure 7 shows the error distribution across the operational workspace and a wide range of orientations. The left panel averages errors in 20 equally spaced depth bins after excluding the outer 1% of depth values; the right panels average within a 32 × 32 grid of horizontal and vertical viewing angles, with unsupported cells masked. The isolated positional-RMSE peak around z ≃0.48 m is a single, mixed-configuration depth bin rather than a controlled range sweep. It combines range with off-axis viewing angle and target scale, so the available analysis cannot assign a unique physical cause. It is therefore interpreted as a local coverage weakness to be targeted in future acquisition, rather than evidence of a monotonic distance failure.

blocks.html: Physical docking experiments were performed with a UR10e manipulator equipped with the active SIROM unit. The passive connector was placed randomly within the reachable workspace, and docking attempts were conducted under varying lighting conditions and partial occlusions. Trials included perturbations in orientation and translation across the whole working area.

Autonomous demonstrations were conducted under progressively challenging conditions involving cluttered placement, dynamic human-induced motion, and elevated and tilted configurations. Docking was completed successfully in these cases, confirming robustness and real-time reliability under cluttered, dynamic, and geometrically challenging conditions.

The demonstrations were not designed as a controlled end-to-end timing benchmark: search distance, target pose, and introduced perturbations differed between them. We therefore report hardware-specific visual-update rates and the 0.33–1.33 s nominal confidence-evidence windows above, but do not claim a pooled time-to-dock statistic. Future trials will log search, approach, alignment, and capture durations separately, together with success rate and final residual pose error.

We presented a lightweight, marker-free subsystem for SIROM autonomous docking. A CNN–Transformer architecture with symmetry-aware quaternion loss enables robust multi-view fusion and resolves rotational ambiguities inherent to the SIROM connector. Temporal smoothing, adaptive pose weighting, and a stability-aware control loop provide consistent real-time performance under partial occlusion and variable illumination.

The held-out test set gives 8.431 mm translation RMSE and 0.0986 rad rotation RMSE, improving to approximately 5 mm and 0.05 rad near the docking decision distance. The visibility output is trained from explicit targetpresent/target-absent labels and prevents low-confidence poses from satisfying the final docking gate.

The fiducial-marker SIROM system of [2] provides a relevant complementary reference. It uses a calibrated marker board, an eye-in-hand camera, and a controller combining position-based visual servoing with an admittance-based force-control phase for final alignment. Our dual-camera approach removes the marker board and learns the target appearance, at the cost of target-specific data collection and an accelerator for inference. A direct accuracy or docking-time ranking would not be valid without matched cameras, workspace, controller, and test protocol.

The system achieves millimeter-level translational and degree-level rotational precision without fiducials, depth sensing, or heavyweight models, demonstrating that reliable autonomous docking can be achieved with a lightweight architecture.
The data used in training consist exclusively of nonpersonal laboratory imagery, and no human-related or sensitive information was involved.

For manuscript preparation, generative AI tools were used solely for language editing and clarity improvement. They were not involved in experimental design, data analysis, or scientific reasoning. The authors retain full responsibility for the content.
